guide.summary: Unit 4 covers the civil rights movement, Black Power and the Black Arts Movement, Black feminism and intersectionality, the founding of Black studies, Pan-African and diasporic connections, and contemporary debates over housing, incarceration, reparations, and activism such as Black Lives Matter.

sections.heading: The civil rights movement
sections.body: The NAACP's legal strategy, led by Thurgood Marshall, won Brown v. Board of Education (1954), overturning 'separate but equal' in public schools. The 1955 murder of Emmett Till, and his mother Mamie Till-Mobley's decision to hold an open-casket funeral, galvanized national outrage. The Montgomery bus boycott (1955–56), sparked by Rosa Parks's arrest and organized by local activists and the Montgomery Improvement Association led by Martin Luther King Jr., ended with a court ruling against bus segregation. Federal troops escorted the Little Rock Nine into Central High (1957). Student sit-ins began in Greensboro (1960), and SNCC formed that year with support from Ella Baker, who championed grassroots, group-centered leadership rather than reliance on a single charismatic leader. CORE's Freedom Rides (1961) tested desegregation of interstate travel. The Birmingham campaign (1963), King's Letter from Birmingham Jail defending direct action, and the March on Washington (1963) built pressure for the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Freedom Summer (1964) organized voter registration in Mississippi; Fannie Lou Hamer of the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party testified about violence against voters. The Selma marches and 'Bloody Sunday' (1965) led to the Voting Rights Act of 1965. The Fair Housing Act followed in 1968.

sections.heading: Black Power, culture, and Black feminism
sections.body: Malcolm X, a Nation of Islam minister until 1964, argued for Black self-determination and self-defense and criticized integration as the main goal; after his pilgrimage to Mecca he embraced a broader, internationalist outlook before his assassination in 1965. Stokely Carmichael popularized 'Black Power' in 1966, emphasizing racial pride, community control, and independent political organization. The Black Panther Party (Oakland, 1966) combined armed patrols monitoring police with community programs such as free breakfasts for children, and became a target of FBI surveillance (COINTELPRO). The Black Arts Movement, associated with Amiri Baraka, created art by and for Black communities. Student strikes, notably at San Francisco State (1968–69), led to the first Black studies programs and ethnic studies colleges. Black feminists argued that racism, sexism, and class oppression are interconnected: the Combahee River Collective Statement (1977) made this case, and legal scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw later coined 'intersectionality' (1989). Shirley Chisholm became the first Black woman elected to Congress (1968) and ran for president in 1972.

sections.heading: Diaspora and contemporary debates
sections.body: Pan-Africanism linked Black struggles worldwide: Pan-African Congresses, the Négritude movement of Aimé Césaire and Léopold Senghor, and African independence movements (Ghana in 1957) inspired and were inspired by U.S. activists. Contemporary debates include: residential segregation and the wealth gap, rooted partly in redlining by federal mapping and lending policies in the 1930s; mass incarceration, which Michelle Alexander's The New Jim Crow (2010) compares to earlier systems of racial control; reparations, including H.R. 40, a bill to study reparations first introduced by Rep. John Conyers in 1989; and policing. Black Lives Matter began in 2013, founded by Alicia Garza, Patrisse Cullors, and Opal Tometi after the acquittal in Trayvon Martin's killing, and grew into mass protests in 2020 after the murder of George Floyd. Barack Obama's election in 2008 prompted debate over whether the U.S. had become 'post-racial.' Afrofuturism, seen in the fiction of Octavia Butler, imagines Black futures through science fiction and art.

keyTakeaways: Civil rights gains came through litigation, direct action, and grassroots organizing.
Leaders disagreed over nonviolence, integration, and self-defense.
Black Power stressed pride, self-determination, and community control.
The movement was connected to global anticolonial struggles.
Debates continue over wealth gaps, incarceration, reparations, and policing.
commonMistakes: Presenting the movement as only King and Parks; local organizers and women such as Ella Baker and Fannie Lou Hamer were central.
Confusing the Civil Rights Act (1964) with the Voting Rights Act (1965).
Describing Black Power only as violent; it included political, cultural, and community programs.
Treating Malcolm X's views as unchanging.
Treating the movement as ending in 1968.
examTips: Compare strategies precisely: legal, nonviolent direct action, electoral, nationalist.
Explain how legal changes (Brown, 1964, 1965) did not end economic inequality.
Use specific contemporary evidence (redlining, H.R. 40, BLM) for later-period questions.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Describe one goal shared by the civil rights movement and the Black Power movement.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Explain one difference between the strategies of the civil rights movement and the Black Power movement.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Explain how Black women activists shaped either movement.

rubric.description: E.g., ending racial discrimination, securing political power and voting rights, improving economic conditions, dignity for Black Americans.
E.g., nonviolence and integration (sit-ins, marches, legislation) vs self-defense, community control, independent Black institutions (Panthers, Carmichael).

E.g., Ella Baker and SNCC's grassroots model; Fannie Lou Hamer and the MFDP; Rosa Parks and boycott organizing; women's leadership in Panther community programs; Black feminist critiques like Combahee.

practice.sampleResponse:
A. Both movements sought to end racial oppression and give Black Americans real political power, such as the ability to vote and influence local government.

B. The civil rights movement mainly used nonviolent direct action and pushed for integration and federal laws like the Voting Rights Act, while Black Power groups such as the Black Panthers stressed self-defense and community control through independent institutions.

C. Ella Baker shaped the civil rights movement by helping found SNCC and promoting group-centered leadership, which trained local people to organize voter registration in places like Mississippi instead of relying on national leaders.
